title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: Parvati goes into the forest to win Shiva by her own austerity, and a young ascetic shows up to tell her she's wasting her life

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, spring came out of season, and Kama was burned to ash by the third eye. Desire forced from outside couldn't win Shiva. Which want did you let pass? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

A princess takes off her jewels. She sets aside her silk and puts on bark. She leaves her father's palace and walks up into the mountains, to a place where Shiva once sat, and she begins. In the Shiva Purana, Parvati has seen what happened to Kama. Beauty didn't win Shiva. Help from the gods didn't win him. So she'll do what Shiva himself does. She'll practice tapas. And one day, deep into it, a visitor comes up the path: a young ascetic with matted hair and a staff, who sits down and asks, very politely, what on earth she thinks she's doing.
screen: `JEWELS OFF, BARK ON.` → `SHE'LL DO WHAT SHIVA DOES.` → `A VISITOR COMES UP THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Tapas is austerity, disciplined effort that burns away what's easy and leaves what's strong. In the story, Parvati's tapas grows harder and harder. She stands in the cold, and sits among fires in the heat. She eats less, and then less again, and tradition says she gave up even fallen leaves, which is why one of her names is Aparna. Her mother had begged her not to go. She keeps on. Then the visitor. He's courteous at first. Then he starts in on Shiva. Why this one? He smears himself with ash from cremation grounds. He wears snakes. He rides a bull. Nobody knows his family. He has no house, no money, and he burned the god of love. A woman like you, he says, could marry anyone. Parvati's answer is the heart of the selection. She doesn't argue with the facts. She says, in effect, that the visitor doesn't know who Shiva is. What looks poor and strange from outside is exactly what she loves. And she won't sit and listen to him being insulted. She gets up to leave. Then the visitor changes. He drops the disguise, and it's Shiva himself, who came to test her and found her immovable. Remember Sati, who would not hear her husband mocked. Parvati, born again, will not hear it either. Same loyalty, a second life. And where Kama's arrow failed, her own tapas succeeds. Shiva agrees to marry her. So the Shiva Purana's answer to yesterday is simple: what can't be forced from outside can be won by steady effort from within.
screen: `TAPAS: EFFORT THAT BURNS CLEAN.` · `SHE GAVE UP EVEN LEAVES.` · `THE VISITOR MOCKS SHIVA.` · `SHE WON'T LISTEN, AND IT'S HIM.` · then, large: `WON FROM WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: a small tapas. For this sit, choose one thing to hold steady, and hold it. Your posture, or your gaze, or simply staying with the breath and not drifting into plans. Settle, and begin. When the mind tries to wander off, come back, without scolding. That coming back is the effort. If a voice starts in, telling you this is pointless, notice it, the way Parvati noticed the visitor, and stay put. If you pray, you can repeat Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as your steady point. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: Parvati's tapas, the visitor who mocked Shiva, and the loyalty that turned out to be the test.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Today, pick one small effort and keep it going even after a voice tells you to quit. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus tell Parvati's tapas and her marriage to Shiva in the Shiva Purana and in poetry; some women keep fasts in her honor, such as Hartalika Teej, praying for a good marriage or for their husbands' welfare.

notes: Selection four (Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda). Paraphrased details to confirm: Parvati setting aside ornaments for bark; going to the place of Shiva's earlier meditation; standing in cold, sitting among fires in heat; giving up even fallen leaves, hence Aparna ('tradition says'); Mena begging her to stop; the disguised ascetic (brahmachari/jatila) listing Shiva's oddities including burning Kama; Parvati's refusal to listen and rising to leave; Shiva revealing himself and agreeing to marry her.
Aparna as 'one who gave up even leaves' is a traditional etymology, attributed with 'tradition says'; confirm it is in the Shiva Purana or move to Kalidasa/Puranic tradition generally.
Trapdoor floor 3 links tapas to heat (root tap-, to heat): standard lexicon; confirm.
howItsDone names Hartalika Teej as a fast in Parvati's honor; confirm phrasing and regional scope.
1122–1124 (further Shiva Purana selections) belong to another writer; the marriage itself is left for them.
